new_statements.quote: A phonological word consists of one or more syllables with word stress always occurring on the ultimate syllable. In bisyllabic or trisyllabic words the syllables preceding the stress are voiceless and/or accelerated, accentuating the Chatino trend towards using only monosyllabic words. Tri-syllabic words are very unusual. (p. 248) — Tone is only significant on word-final syllables and thus only the final syllable of a word has tone marked in this work. (p. 9)
new_statements.citation: Pride, Kitty (1965). Chatino syntax. Norman: Summer Institute of Linguistics of the University of Oklahoma. 249 pp.
new_statements.locator: Appendix C 'A note on phonological words', p. 248 (PDF page 250); Introduction §0, p. 9 (PDF page 11) and p. 10 (PDF page 12); §3.7, p. 69 (PDF page 71)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (256 PDF pages, text) and the. PDF page 250 = book p. 248, Appendix C 'A NOTE ON PHONOLOGICAL WORDS': 'A phonological word consists of one or more syllables with word stress always occurring on the ultimate syllable. In bisyllabic or trisyllabic words the syllables preceding the stress are voiceless and/or accelerated, accentuating the Chatino trend towards using only monosyllabic words. Tri-syllabic words are very unusual.' — verbatim. Same page: Spanish loans 'The stress maybe [sic] shifted to the ultimate syllable and the initial syllables become voiceless, accelerated, or contracted to a consonant cluster' (panela > pnela, semana > smno, machete > wstyi), or split into a phonolog…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (StressTyp2 rule 01/001/0001.., i.e. fixed final): Pride states word stress is always on the ultimate syllable. It also refines the record by adding that the language is tonal with tone contrastive only on that final stressed syllable, that pretonic syllables are voiceless/accelerated, and that Spanish loans are re-stressed to the final syllable. Describes the Yaitepec dialect, which belongs to Western Highland Chatino (ISO ctp, west2644).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress always falls on the last syllable of the phonological word; the syllables before the stressed final are voiceless and/or accelerated (reduced), so words tend to be monosyllabic and trisyllables are rare. Tone (four registers plus glides) is contrastive only on the word-final, i.e. stressed, syllable. At phrase level the single phrase stress falls on the major word; monosyllabic minor words carry only minor word stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None at word level. Phrase level: 'minor words are monosyllabic and occur only in expanded phrases, clauses, or sentences, where they never carry the phrase or sentence stress, but only minor word stress' (p. 10); 'The single phrase stress always occurs on the major word in the expression' (p. 69).
new_statements.exceptions: Spanish loanwords of more than one syllable are conformed to the pattern: 'The stress may be shifted to the ultimate syllable and the initial syllables become voiceless, accelerated, or contracted to a consonant cluster' (panela > pnela, semana > smno, machete > wstyi), or the loan is split into a two-word phonological phrase (tienda > tiye ta, culantro > kula ntru) (p. 248). Footnote p. 9 warns that ongoing work on suprasegmentals 'will probably present an alternative solution involving the relationship between stress, tone, and vowel length'; the tone-perturbation system was unsolved at the time.
new_statements.identity_note: Pride 1965 explicitly describes the Yaitepec dialect ('There are at least three distinct and mutually unintelligible dialects with centres in the towns of Yaitepec, Taltaltepec, and Zenzontepec. This work deals with the Yaitepec dialect', p. 9). Santiago Yaitepec Chatino is part of Western Highland Chatino (ISO 639-3 ctp = west2644), so the statement applies to this catalog item. Note that the archive.org Rosetta Project excerpt is filed under the code 'cta' (Tataltepec), which is a mislabel of the archive item, not of the work. The full scan is the University of Florida copy (archive.org id chatinosyntax00prid).

new_statements.citation: McKaughan, Howard P. 1954. Chatino formulas and phonemes. International Journal of American Linguistics 20(1): 23-27.
new_statements.check: reported on verification, not yet confirmed
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: McKaughan 1954 (index 0), marked not accessible by the compiler, is in fact openly available: archive.org item sim_international-journal-of-american-linguistics_1954-01_20_1 (IJAL 20(1), January 1954, no access restriction; saved). I read the article (pp. 23-27) in full: it is a phonemics paper (consonant-sequence formulas, consonants, vowels, four tone registers) and contains NO statement about stress or accent; the only prosody-adjacent remarks are fn. 2 (most Chatino words are monosyllabic) and sec. 4 on tone (four registers: high, mid-high, mid-low, low, with voiceless high-vowel allophones 'tentatively defined as absence of tone'). It does confirm the languoid (Yaitepec dialect, fn. 1)…

tone_statements.quote: The SJQ tonal system has the following characteristics, as shown by Table 21: … A. Ten tones. Four are level tones, L, M, H, and S(uperhigh); four are rising, LM, LH, MH, and MS; and two are falling, HL and ML. … B. The tone-bearing unit is the syllable, which is monomoraic. Furthermore, non-compound words are monosyllabic (except certain loans, see Cruz 2011). C. Each (non-compound) word hosts one of only about 14 possible TONE SEQUENCES, despite the large tone inventory. … But the TS’s are much simpler, consisting of just one linking tone and, optionally, one floating tone.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 103-104, sec. 5.3.1 'The SJQ tonal system in the context of comparative Chatino tone', points A-C
tone_statements.summary: San Juan Quiahije Chatino: ten tones (level L M H superhigh; rising LM LH MH MS; falling HL ML) on monosyllabic words, syllable the TBU; a word hosts one linked tone plus an optional floating tone.

Provide acoustic description of 11 basic tones in SJQ. … H+0 is a tone similar to H tone, but it has a phonemic floating tone … +H is a pre-linked floating tone … This speaker merges all three falling tones in isolation

tone_statements.quote: Like other Zapotecan languages, QC features lexical tone; however the inventory of Eastern Chatino tone categories and sandhi rules is much larger than those of other Zapotecan languages. … QC has fourteen phonemic tone categories. Each is composed of up to two of the four tonal primitives in the language (L M H and the superhigh 0) and may be associated with one of two unlinked floating tones (+H or +0). Table (1) shows the inventory of tones in QC. Table 1: The Tonemes of QC (from Cruz (2011:124))
tone_statements.locator: sec. 1.1 and sec. 1.2.1 'Cruz (2011) for simplex words' with Table 1; no page numbers
tone_statements.summary: Lexical tone: 14 phonemic categories (level, rising, falling) from primitives L, M, H, superhigh plus floating +H/+0, one per monosyllabic stem; reanalysed as early- vs late-aligned pitch targets.

tone_statements.quote: Among the simplex tones of SJQ1 are three rising contour tones 20, 42 and 402; three falling contour tones 14, 24, and 04; eight linear tones (which may be steady rises or falls) 0, 10, 1, 2, 3, 32, weak 4 and strong 4; and one falling-rising tone 140. Complicating the matter of tone in SJQ are the presence of floating tones and the processes of sandhi which convert some tones … into different tones in particular contexts. … SJQ Chatino is described with five tone levels, 0-4, with 0 representing a rather high tone.

tone_statements.summary: Fifteen simplex tones on five pitch levels (0 high to 4 low): linear 0, 10, 1, 2, 3, 32, weak 4, strong 4; rising 20, 42, 40; falling 14, 24, 04; fall-rise 140; floating tones and tone sandhi.

tone_statements.citation: Cruz, Emiliana & Anthony C. Woodbury. 2006. El sandhi de los tonos en el Chatino de Quiahije. In: Las memorias del Congreso de Idiomas Indígenas de Latinoamérica-II (CILLA II, University of Texas at Austin, 27-29 October 2005). Austin: Archive of the Indigenous Languages of Latin America.
tone_statements.quote: (3) La unidad que lleva el tono es la sílaba/raíz. Entonces, toda sílaba/raíz lleva un tono. … En esa investigación se calculó que la lengua tiene 10 tonos distintos en aislamiento: cuatro tonos nivelados (1, 2, 3, 4; donde tono 1 es el más alto y tono 4 es el más bajo); cuatro tonos ascendentes (20, 32, 40, y 42; donde “0” marca un tono súper-alto); y dos tonos descendentes (14, 24).
tone_statements.translation: (3) The unit that bears the tone is the syllable/root. So every syllable/root bears a tone. … In that research it was calculated that the language has 10 distinct tones in isolation: four level tones (1, 2, 3, 4; where tone 1 is the highest and tone 4 the lowest); four rising tones (20, 32, 40 and 42; where '0' marks a super-high tone); and two falling tones (14, 24).
tone_statements.locator: p. 2, §1.1 'Principios morfofonológicos' item (3) and §2 'Tonos en aislamiento'
tone_statements.summary: Ten tones on monosyllabic roots (syllable = root = TBU): level 1-4 (1 highest), rising 20, 32, 40, 42 (0 super-high), falling 14, 24; floating super-high tone drives rich sandhi; weak/strong 4 and 24.

sources.quote: Like other Zapotecan languages, QC features lexical tone; however the inventory of Eastern Chatino tone categories and sandhi rules is much larger than those of other Zapotecan languages. … QC has fourteen phonemic tone categories. Each is composed of up to two of the four tonal primitives in the language (L M H and the superhigh 0) and may be associated with one of two unlinked floating tones (+H or +0). Table (1) shows the inventory of tones in QC. Table 1: The Tonemes of QC (from Cruz (2011:124))

sources.quote: Among the simplex tones of SJQ1 are three rising contour tones 20, 42 and 402; three falling contour tones 14, 24, and 04; eight linear tones (which may be steady rises or falls) 0, 10, 1, 2, 3, 32, weak 4 and strong 4; and one falling-rising tone 140. Complicating the matter of tone in SJQ are the presence of floating tones and the processes of sandhi which convert some tones … into different tones in particular contexts. … SJQ Chatino is described with five tone levels, 0-4, with 0 representing a rather high tone.

sources.quote: (3) La unidad que lleva el tono es la sílaba/raíz. Entonces, toda sílaba/raíz lleva un tono. … En esa investigación se calculó que la lengua tiene 10 tonos distintos en aislamiento: cuatro tonos nivelados (1, 2, 3, 4; donde tono 1 es el más alto y tono 4 es el más bajo); cuatro tonos ascendentes (20, 32, 40, y 42; donde “0” marca un tono súper-alto); y dos tonos descendentes (14, 24).

tone.translation: (3) The unit that bears the tone is the syllable/root. So every syllable/root bears a tone. … In that research it was calculated that the language has 10 distinct tones in isolation: four level tones (1, 2, 3, 4; where tone 1 is the highest and tone 4 the lowest); four rising tones (20, 32, 40 and 42; where '0' marks a super-high tone); and two falling tones (14, 24).

tone.quote: 1.1. 3rd person simplex verb stems in the completive aspect fall into six main tone groups (forms are glossed with Spanish infinitives and identified according to the comparative tone "Juegos" of Woodbury 2008): 4 (Juego A) 14 (Juego B) 2 (Juego C) 1 (Juego E) 3 (Juego F) 42 (Juego G) … 1.2. In addition, two other tone groupings occur sporadically: 20 (Juego H) 32 (Juego I) … transformed, generally to a tone that either bears a super-high floating tone (10, 14), incorporates a superhigh (20), or is a typical sandhi-derived product (32, 24).
